author: Roy Santa Croce
title: Rutland doctor remembered with marble statue - NewsBreak
text:
By Roy Santa Croce ,
1 hours ago
RUTLAND, VT (ABC22/FOX44) – There is a new public statue in Rutland, honoring a local doctor who was instrumental in identifying the polio epidemic. This marks the 13th statue on the Rutland Sculpture Trail, which started in 2017 as a way to highlight people from the region.
The statue depicts Charles Caverly, who was a doctor in Rutland County starting in 1894. His research into polio led to the development of a vaccine for the entire world.
The marble statue was unveiled earlier in the week, on the lawn of Trinity Episcopal Church.
In the late 1800’s doctors had been reporting small clusters of infant paralysis in the U.S. though, the clusters were so small and sporadic that uncovering a diagnosis seemed impossible.
Charles Caverly is noted for identifying the first, true epidemic of polio in the Otter Valley. Caverly was able to trace 123 people with the disease and noticed most of the victims were children.
“The amount of impact that these Vermonters have had, not just in the area that they’ve served, but across the entire country and really across the entire world,” says Noel Sinozich, executive director of the Carving Studio Sculpture Center.
Back then, the disease hadn’t been coined as polio. It was referred to as infantile paralysis.
the polio virus wouldn’t be identified until 1909.
Caverly was born and raised here in Vermont. He attended Brandon High School, and Dartmouth College before getting his medical degree from UVM.
“And I think it’s important for us as Vermonters to really lift those people up. And for us to remember that people from this tiny, little, not very populous state, can have an absolutely massive impact worldwide,” says Sinozich.
The statue of Caverly was carved by Italian sculptor, Alessandro Lombardo. We also got a preview of the Sculpture Trail’s next, upcoming project, which is a statue honoring three people involved in the annual Gift of Life Blood Drive.
The artist, Evan Morse has made several statues for the trail already and hopes to unveil that monument next month; “and the fact that Rutland has now over a dozen sculptures on the sculpture trail is incredibly impressive. and really speaks to the strength of the community here, and I’m proud to be a part of it,” says Morse.
The polio epidemic plagued Rutland in 1910 and another outbreak in Montpelier seven years later. By then Caverly was the president of the Vermont State Board of Health and instituted home quarantines and banned large public gatherings.
The statue was funded through the Rutland Health Foundation, staff at the Rutland Regional Medical Center, the Rutland City Rotary and other donors.
The great irony of doctor Caverly’s life is that he succumbed to another epidemic that hit Rutland, the influenza pandemic in 1918. He died at 62 years old.
